title: Vertical vs Scale-Out Graph Architecture
description: Toggle between one large graph server and a three-shard cluster, and see why a cross-shard edge costs so much more.
creator: Systems Thinking in the Age of AI
author: Dan McCreary
subject: Systems Thinking in the Age of AI
Graph Database Architecture

educational.learningObjective: Given a growing graph dataset, the learner will compare a single graph-optimized-hardware server against a distributed scale-out cluster and identify why a cross-server edge traversal costs more than a local one.
prerequisites: Knows what a graph traversal is
Has a rough sense that network calls are slower than memory access
learningOutcomes: Compare vertical scaling against scale-out for graph workloads
Explain why a cross-shard traversal costs orders of magnitude more than a local one
Recognize that shard placement is a design decision with performance consequences
educational.assessmentOpportunity: Give learners a small graph and three shards and ask them to assign vertices so as to minimize cross-shard edges, then to justify the assignment.

pedagogical.interactionPattern: View toggle with hover inspection and a highlight mode
pedagogical.instructionalStrategy: Contrasting representations of one identical dataset
pedagogical.feedbackType: Hover explanations naming the cost of each specific hop
misconceptionsAddressed: That distributing a database always improves performance
That all edges in a sharded graph cost the same to traverse
discussionQuestions: Why is sharding a graph harder than sharding a table of independent rows?
What kinds of queries would make the cluster's extra memory worth the cross-shard cost?
Is there a workload where the single server simply cannot win?
